title: The Shallows
sources: search snippets on Chapter 9 'Search, Memory' (study guides)

facts.claim: The Shallows: What the Internet Is Doing to Our Brains (W. W. Norton, 2010) grew out of Carr's 2008 Atlantic essay 'Is Google Making Us Stupid?'

Carr writes that for some years he has had an uncomfortable sense that someone or something has been tinkering with his brain. His concentration drifts after a page or two where he once immersed himself in long prose.
He quotes Bruce Friedman, a blogger on computers in medicine, who says he has almost totally lost the ability to read and absorb a longer text; Friedman: 'I can't read War and Peace anymore.'

Carr argues the brain is plastic: it adapts to what it is repeatedly asked to do; a skill exercised strengthens, one neglected weakens. His examples include monkeys using tools, violinists and London taxi drivers who build detailed mental maps.
Hypertext research: evaluating links adds mental work unrelated to reading; Carr says research favors linear text for comprehension, retention and learning.

Chapter 9 ('Search, Memory'): Carr uses Eric Kandel's early-1970s experiments on the sea slug Aplysia to show that moving information from short-term to long-term memory changes synapses (more synaptic terminals, triggered by serotonin).

Consolidation depends on attention. Kandel is quoted: 'For a memory to persist, the incoming information must be thoroughly and deeply processed.' Carr: 'The key to memory consolidation is attentiveness.'
Working memory is small; long-term memory can expand and contract almost without limit by growing and pruning synaptic terminals.

Carr: the Web is a convenient supplement to personal memory, but when we use it as a substitute and bypass the inner processes of consolidation, we risk emptying our minds of their riches. He denies that computer memory and human memory are equivalent.
Carr says that writing about his days helps him remember them better.

1681.note: Carr's own reading drift, Friedman's confession, plasticity examples (taxi drivers, monkeys, violinists) without inflating to proof of damage. Medium confidence, secondary sources.
